It made its live TV debut at the 41st Stellar Gospel Music Awards. At a listening party in Atlanta on Oct. 12, according to Hot 100.9, Franklin said, “I’ve never done a double album before.” He described the TobyMac collaboration “It Gets Better” as “my attempt to find a space to talk about mental health,” and added, “I’ve had my own journey with anxiety and depression.” He also talked about changes in the Black church. “The Black church culture changed,” he said. “The church got rid of their choirs and the music was in a space that was not my strength.” He had advice for emerging artists, too. “Start off very true and build your audience slow,” he said. “Don’t ride the trends because you don’t know when they’re coming.”

articles.content: San Antonio Spurs rookie Tarris Reed Jr. got baptized days after making his NBA debut, and he posted the video to Instagram under two words: “Jesus Saves.” Reed, a 23-year-old center, was the No. 26 pick in this year’s draft out of UConn. Denver took him, and San Antonio acquired him in a trade. He debuted on Tuesday, Oct. 20, in a 116-104 loss to the Oklahoma City Thunder. In the caption, Reed wrote that he got home late after his first NBA back-to-back and “got my first real glimpse of just how grueling the 82-game NBA season can be.” On the plane ride, he remembered it was Baptism Sunday at his church. “I texted Pastor Ed, and the rest was history LOL.” “It’s been on my heart for a while now to be baptized,” Reed wrote. “I wanted to publicly signify my union with Christ and what it means to walk in His grace, mercy, and NEWNESS OF LIFE!” He quoted Romans 6:4: “We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life.” He also wrote about what he sees coming next. “The Lord has placed me in a unique position to help others come to know Christ and experience His life changing power,” he wrote. “To think that I went from wanting nothing to do with the Lord to now desiring to live for Him is something I never could have imagined. I never would have thought my life would look like this.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by TRJ (@iamtarrisreed) Reed is a St. Louis native who started his college career at Michigan, transferred to UConn after his sophomore year and was the Big East Sixth Man of the Year as a junior. In April, UConn lost the national title game to Michigan, and Reed went to Instagram afterward. “I’ve been wrestling with God about this all day” , he wrote in a post that week. “Losing the biggest game of my entire basketball career hurts,” he said. “I tend to be a perfectionist, but only Jesus was perfect.” He wrote that he felt Jesus put it on his heart to go to an Athletes in Action meeting and speak, even though he didn’t want to. He barely had time to prepare, so he told himself he would let the Holy Spirit speak through him. “That night, two of the women’s basketball players got baptized,” he wrote. “It’s not my will, it’s His.” His October post ended with “All glory to God!”

articles.title_zh: 卡尔和劳拉·伦茨谈论五年的公开判断： “你不能从我们的故事中看不到上帝”
articles.content: Five years ago, Laura Lentz had more advice than she wanted. People who had never met her were telling her what to do about her husband, her marriage and her future. “Getting all these opinions and judgments from the outside when no one really knows what’s going on,” she says. “Only the people that are in this know what it takes.” In November 2020, Hillsong founder Brian Houston told staff that Carl Lentz was out at the church’s Manhattan campus, citing breaches of trust. An extramarital affair had come to light. Laura, who had done nothing to land in that spotlight, found herself in it anyway. This month the two of them released a book, Overcoming Infidelity: 10 Conversations To Help Heal the Hurt , and the couple sat down with us to talk about how they got from there to here. “I struggled with a lot of anxiety and just struggling with the opinions of others,” Laura says. “I had to really make sure that didn’t get in here and just remind myself that this is what matters and only we know what’s going on. Lots of therapy has been great. And Jesus, of course, helping through this.” The criticism hasn’t ended, but she says it has changed. “Now I find that’s really gotten quite silent. I think the fruit of our relationship and the fruit of our kids’ lives and where we are now and even writing the book, like you can’t not see God through our story. You can’t not see the miracle through our story.” She is clear about what the book is not. “We’re not out here promoting the book like we’re out to save marriages,” she says. “It’s about me healing, him healing and seeing where that takes us.” The Secrets That Started Small Asked what signs a young married couple should watch for, both of them go to the same place: secrets. “It’s not just big secrets, it’s like the little things,” Laura says. “If you can’t be honest or you’re hiding things from your spouse, those are dangerous and they just compound.” She remembers praying in the weeks before everything surfaced. “I don’t know what it is, but God, you’ve got to get this, just get it out.” Carl says the distance did not begin with the affair. “You don’t start keeping secrets about cheating. You start keeping secrets about fear.” He describes deciding what his wife could handle and keeping the pressure to himself. “It’s when I made the decisions for her on what she was capable of holding,” he says. “Then you stack them and you stack them. By the time you get to the horrific stuff, you’ve already got a pattern of hiding stuff.” What he tells young men now is blunt: get used to being vulnerable with your wife. “It turns out it’s very attractive.” He also rejects the idea that pastors have nobody to tell. “If anybody ever says ‘I didn’t have anybody to be open with,’ I lovingly say I don’t believe you. You chose to not tell anybody.” He says that if he had called Houston on a bad day, he would have been flown out to help. “I did not call. I was not honest. That’s on me.” What Staying Actually Looked Like People tell the spouse who stays that she is brave. Laura is not sure that’s the right word. “It’s so hard to stay, it’s so hard to go,” she says. “Yes, I was brave, I guess, but I was also taking a risk.” She says she would never tell someone to stay in an adulterous relationship, and that she herself saw evidence of change before she did. “There’s gotta be evidence of things that are changing for you to stay and he’s gotta be doing his work.” She describes the early days in small units of time. “We literally went one day at a time. I would wake up and go, okay, I can do today. And that was it.” Carl, a basketball fan, says she has learned the language for it. “Every day, I’m on a one-day contract. That’s an upgrade from a two-hour contract that I was on for quite a long time.” The marriage that came out of that, Laura says, is not the one they had before. “Marriage 2.0 is like so much deeper. articles.title: Meet Elle Limebear, the British Artist Who Turned a School-Assembly Hymn Into a UK No. 1
articles.summary: The daughter of Delirious? frontman Martin Smith rebuilt “Oil in My Lamp” for a new generation, and “Give Me Joy” has spent nine weeks atop the UK Christian chart.
articles.summary_zh: Delirious主唱马丁·史密斯（ Martin Smith ）的女儿为新一代重建了“Oil in My Lamp” ， “Give Me Joy”在英国基督教排行榜上排名第九。
articles.title_zh: 认识英国艺术家Elle Limebear ，他将学校集会赞美诗变成了英国第一
articles.content: Elle Limebear used to have a hard time describing her dad’s job. When classmates asked what he did, she’d say he was in a band, then that it was Christian music, then that it was sort of rocky, and then she’d watch the conversation go nowhere. Some days she wished he were “just a plumber dad.” Her father is Martin Smith, the frontman of Delirious?, the British band behind “History Maker” and “Did You Feel the Mountains Tremble?” and one of the defining worship bands of the late ‘90s and 2000s. She remembers touring the US as a kid, on big tour buses, with people lining up for photos with him. Back home in their English village, “no one really cared.” Limebear now lives in Brighton with her husband, Tom, and their three young children, and the song she’s best known for is one almost every British adult has sung. “Give Me Joy,” released in July, reworks the hymn “Oil in My Lamp.” It debuted at No. 1 on the Official UK Christian & Gospel Singles Chart and has held the top spot for nine weeks since. Decca Records, which announced her signing the same month, calls her its first contemporary Christian artist. The hymn was a fixture of British school assemblies, whether or not the school was religious. “If you sing ‘Oil in My Lamp,’ probably everyone will know it,” Limebear told RELEVANT. “It’s in our childhood. It’s in our bones almost.” She started slipping it into her live sets a few years ago. The reaction surprised her. “There was this eruption of, I know this. I remember being a kid singing this,” she said. “People just belted it, absolutely belted it.” Her husband suggested she rewrite it for people who never grew up singing it. Her first reaction was that the song was already a banner. “What a challenge.” She wrote new verses and melodies and kept the heart of it. When her new label asked whether she had anything to lead with, she figured the answer was no. “It’s a British kind of hymn-like thing,” she said. “Not super cool.” Then she played it for the team, a room of people who, in her words, don’t know Jesus. “They absolutely loved it and it brought them alive. They’re like, I remember singing this song.” The song was only a chorus and a verse at that point, and the response is what pushed her to finish it. Limebear never planned to be a songwriter. At 20 she was set on photography, which felt safe. “I could contain it, control it,” she said. Then she felt God tell her, clearly, to do music. “It didn’t feel like my thought.” She says fear kept her from believing she had anything to bring, and she didn’t know how to write songs. “Back then I was definitely hesitantly walking through these doors full of fear. Now I feel like I’m skipping through them.” The version of England she’s skipping through is a different one from the England she grew up in. She was the only Christian in her whole school, she said, and her youth group “saved my life.” Lately she hears from friends and church leaders across the country about people walking into church out of plain curiosity about Jesus. “There’s this thing called the quiet revival that they say is going on,” she said, “where people are just finding him in all sorts of places.” She remembers being the weirdest person in the room for it. Now, she says, people are discovering that “actually, being a Christian isn’t that weird.” Her takeaway for believers is the same one. “I think we should all be more curious, even as Christians,” she said. “Get more curious. Ask more questions.” Asked what’s behind it, she didn’t pretend to know. “I don’t know is the answer.” She pointed to decades of quiet prayer, from older women in church prayer meetings to families praying at home for relatives to come to faith, and added: “God hears every prayer, doesn’t he?” and “nothing’s wasted.” She also described the last few years in the Church as “good, sad, confusing,” with “lots of walls” coming down, and says she senses something being built back up that looks different from before. articles.title_zh: 你能在积累财富的同时仍然跟随耶稣吗？是的，但首先定义“足够”。
articles.content: The first decent paycheck can come with an unexpected side of guilt. Maybe your salary no longer starts with a 4, or your savings finally hit a number that once sounded rich. The relief is real. So is the question: Am I allowed to want more? For Christians raised to view wealth with suspicion, professional success can feel surprisingly complicated. The paychecks get bigger, but the question of what faithful ambition looks like often goes unanswered. Paige Whitaker thinks the question is worth asking, and that the guilt is pointed at the wrong thing. “I don’t believe wealth and purpose are competing pursuits,” says Whitaker, brand growth and partnerships manager at 316 Financial, a faith-forward bank. “Throughout Scripture, we see faithful people who were blessed with significant resources. The real question is whether we own our money or our money owns us.” Abraham was rich. So were Job, Lydia and Joseph of Arimathea. Scripture doesn’t treat having money and worshiping it as the same thing. Jesus put it plainly: you just can’t serve two. “Wealth becomes dangerous when it becomes our identity, our measure of success, or the thing we rely on most,” Whitaker says. Define “enough” before you get there One practical move: Define enough before your income makes it easy to keep moving the goalposts. “Purpose acts as a guardrail,” Whitaker says. “It helps us define ‘enough’ and reminds us why we’re pursuing financial success in the first place. Without purpose, it’s easy to spend a lifetime chasing bigger numbers while missing what truly matters.” Write it down. A number for the emergency fund. A lifestyle line you won’t cross even when you could. A giving percentage that goes up with your income instead of down. The point is to make the decision once, on purpose, so you’re not renegotiating it with yourself every time a bonus hits. Ask a different set of questions Building wealth with purpose, Whitaker says, starts by changing the questions. Instead of “how do I get more,” ask what the money is for. She points to serving others, providing for family, supporting churches and investing in communities and causes that matter. Run your own money through it. What does your current budget say you care about? If the honest answer is DoorDash and a car payment, that’s data, and now you know what to change. When the increase comes Markeia Johnson leads the Financial Stewardship Committee at 316 Financial, and she gets specific about what to do when the raise actually lands. “When financial increase comes, our response should be guided by prayer and purpose rather than increased spending,” she says. “Additional resources can be used to reduce debt, build savings, invest for the future, support ministry and help those in need.” Notice what’s missing: “upgrade everything.” Lifestyle creep is the quiet way money takes over. Every raise gets absorbed, enough keeps moving, and ten years in you make three times what you did and feel exactly as stretched. “Having the means to make a purchase does not always make it the right decision,” Johnson says. Money as a tool Both return to Matthew 6:33, where Jesus tells His followers to seek God’s kingdom first. “When we seek God’s Kingdom first, money becomes a tool for stewardship rather than a source of security or identity,” Johnson says. “True prosperity is measured not by how much we possess, but by how faithfully we use what God has entrusted to us.” “Money is a tool, not a destination,” Whitaker says. “Wealth is valuable because of what it enables us to do, not because of what it says about us.” Build wealth. Negotiate the raise. Learn how a Roth IRA works. But decide what the money is for before it starts making those decisions for you. “Wealth is a wonderful servant but a terrible master,” Whitaker says. “The goal isn’t simply to build more wealth. The goal is to use what God has entrusted to us to make a meaningful impact.” This article is presented in partnership with 316 Financial, a faith-forward

articles.content: In the NBA, the postgame TV interview moves fast. The horn sounds, the star of the night gets steered toward the sideline and a reporter is waiting with a microphone before he’s caught his breath. After the Toronto Raptors beat the Washington Wizards 112-102 on Friday, Oct. 23, the microphone was ready. But Scottie Barnes was walking across midcourt with a Gatorade towel over his head, headed for the Wizards’ postgame prayer circle. A player in the Washington group waved him over. Barnes stepped in among forward Anthony Gill and a handful of Wizards players, and the circle closed around him. Barnes, Toronto’s 25-year-old forward and a former NBA Rookie of the Year, had just finished with 28 points, 14 rebounds and five assists. Toronto’s TV broadcast, meanwhile, was holding for him. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bleacher Report (@bleacherreport) “He just took off,” one of the Raptors’ broadcasters said as Barnes joined the huddle. “So we’ll wait a minute for him to return.” A few seconds later, the call caught up to the picture: Barnes was “in the huddle there with the Wizards players, sharing a prayer as the Toronto Raptors come away with this victory.” When the circle broke, there were hugs all around, and Barnes started back across the floor with the towel around his neck. “Here comes Scottie,” the broadcast said, sending it down to the sideline. The microphone was still waiting. Gill, in his seventh season with Washington, was one of five finalists for the J. Walter Kennedy Citizenship Award in 2024, which NBA writers give for community service. He has talked publicly about his faith, too. Sharing the stage with Orlando Magic forward Jonathan Isaac at Liberty University’s convocation in 2024 , he told students that people assume an NBA player has “it all figured out.” “They assume that just because you’ve been blessed with a lot of money, life should be easy,” he said. He also said, “I tell myself I need to be more like Jesus. And what was Jesus? The ultimate servant. So, I serve the people around me.”

Demand was there before the first show. Pollstar reported in December that the tour had already passed 470,000 tickets sold. The growth is steep. articles.content:
Ten basic foods now cost more than a week of work in 11 of the 56 countries surveyed in a new
Price Shocks report
from World Vision, and nine of those 11 are in Sub-Saharan Africa. In Sudan, buying them takes 19.3 eight-hour workdays. In Myanmar, 10.1, and in Haiti, 9.5. In the Central African Republic, buying them takes 30.1 days. In the U.S., it takes an hour.
Between November 2025 and May 2026, researchers priced the same ten foods at local markets, shops and supermarkets: a kilogram each of bananas, rice, wheat flour, sugar, maize and tomatoes, a dozen eggs, a liter of cooking oil, a liter of milk and one raw chicken. They then compared the cost of those ten foods with each country’s average income per person, adjusted for purchasing power, to work out how many hours of work it takes to afford them. That is a national average, not a minimum wage, so a lower-paid worker would need even longer.
Average income can hide inequality and may overstate what the poorest families can buy. Four countries with active conflict or collapsed institutions, South Sudan, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela, were left out of the hours analysis because there was no income data to compare, so the survey found bad situations but misses the worst ones.
Sudan shows how hard a conflict zone is to measure. The survey recorded the Sudanese price of the ten foods getting 36 percent cheaper than in 2024, yet the report says famine was present in parts of the country in 2025 and 2026, and Sudan is still one of the least affordable places in the study.
The report also profiles families living with the numbers.
Khin, 45, earns money ironing and washing clothes in Myanmar’s Yangon Region. Her husband can’t work because of poor health, and they have eight children. “There are days when my children eat rice with only oil and salt,” she is quoted as saying. “This is no longer occasional; it has become a daily reality.”
She says her twins are becoming malnourished and having digestive issues. Her 12-year-old daughter, Chit, told the report’s authors that fish and chicken have given way to spinach, tea leaf salad and fermented fish sauce.
In Hinche, Haiti, Cherlande runs a market stall that pays for her children’s school, their clothes and the family’s food, and she says she has no other income. A cup of rice that cost 20 or 25 gourdes now costs 50, she says, and a small packet of spaghetti has gone from 50 gourdes to 100. “You can’t afford to eat meat every day,” she said.
In 2025, an estimated 35.5 million children were acutely malnourished worldwide, nearly 10 million of them severely, according to the Global Report on Food Crises figures the report cites. Malnutrition can damage a child’s physical and cognitive development and weaken immunity, and the effects can last into adulthood.
The report asks governments, donors and businesses to protect children’s access to food during crises, expand school meals and social protection, and invest in local food systems.
Compassion International
works on the same problem from another angle, and says it provides children living in poverty with care that includes meals, tutoring and medical care.
TAKE ACTION
Read the
full report
, pass it to someone who has never thought about groceries in terms of days of work, and pray for the families behind the numbers.

articles.title_zh: 破碎的系统保护贩运者，而不是女孩
articles.content: I’m often asked about the night I spent in a Southeast Asian jail alongside three young girls who had been exploited by sex traffickers. But the primary question isn’t about why I was in jail. Rather, why were those three girls in jail to begin with? Why them, and not the traffickers who had taken them from their families and sold them repeatedly for sex, turning their lives into a brutal nightmare? Why not the woman who had put tape over the mouth of the young girl so that the man who was raping her would not be disturbed by her screams. The system failed them. The brothel keeper was tipped off about their rescue operation, allowed to hide her crime, and told to dump the girls at a nearby bus stop. The police who should have rescued them instead arrested them on immigration charges. The trafficker walked free, while the girls were treated as criminals. As I sat with them that night, I longed for those girls to have never been taken to jail, much less a brothel. I wanted them to have always been at home with their families, going to school, and playing with their friends. I wanted them to have never been harmed in the first place. But the reality is, like millions of women and girls in our world today, they suffered the consequences of a broken justice system. And so, the reason I stayed with the girls is simply that the alternative was just too horrible. I preferred to be arrested myself rather than leave them vulnerable to further assault. But there’s an important detail to clarify: in the end, I did not need to stay the full night. Once it was clear I was not going away, the jailer himself took on the responsibility of assuring their safety. In a broken system, when even just one agent uses their authority for good, the door to justice begins to open. Shifting Power The very next day, my colleagues at International Justice Mission (IJM) and I were able to bring the girls to safety and long-term holistic aftercare. I continued to visit the girls for years, witnessing their healing as they moved into new lives of freedom. But nearly 25 years after that night in jail, the fight remains the same; we must not leave until those with governing power wield their power to protect the most vulnerable. If we fail to intervene for the women and girls being brutalized by violent criminals, including intimate partners and family members, the alternative is unconscionable. But when we do show up, we get to be part of shifting the levers of power. Entire systems – even the most corrupt and unjust – begin to change for good. In the 21st century, we must reckon with the reality that millions of women and girls are still not any more safe from violence than they have been in any previous era. It is still true, as it has been for decades, that one in three women will experience physical or sexual violence in their lifetime. Today, and in fact, every day, 140 women will be killed by their partners or family members. But far too often, law enforcement and other government actors appear to be on the side of violent perpetrators and other abusers, rather than those who are suffering violence. Whether it’s taking bribes to protect traffickers, criminalizing women and children who are being exploited, or allowing them to be intimidated into not reporting the abuse, agents of the law bear tremendous responsibility and opportunity to change the systemic violence they have enabled to perpetuate. Violent crime thrives on opportunity, and the argument for countering this could not be more clear: strengthening justice systems deters violence. When laws are enforced and traffickers and other abusers are held accountable, other perpetrators of violence are discouraged from committing similar crimes. I think of this as flipping the fear equation. When violent abusers begin to fear the consequences of law, women and children begin to live free from fear. articles.title_zh: 研究人员说，雷达显示土耳其船形编队内的房间和走廊，有些人认为是诺亚方舟
articles.content: A radar scientist working at a boat-shaped formation in eastern Turkey says his scans show organized patterns, chambers and corridors inside it, and that those features are not natural rock. The scientist, Khosrow Bakhtar, is a veteran U.S. defense scientist and the inventor of the BakhtarRadar system used at the site, according to the project’s release. He reported the preliminary results from inside the Durupınar Formation, a roughly 515-foot structure near Mount Ararat that Ark hunters have studied since 1959. Bakhtar said the radar was set to mask natural geological signals, so a purely natural anomaly would not have shown up in the processed images. He called it “the most significant finding of 45 years of my career.” Prof. Cenker Atila of Sivas Cumhuriyet University, who oversees the permitted project, reviewed and confirmed the preliminary results, the release says. He added that the radar also shows a structure with three levels, which he compared to the three levels of the Ark in “our Holy Books.” The findings were presented at a symposium in Turkey, and the group, Noah’s Ark Scans, announced them this week. The group also reports recovering charred wood from almost 30 feet down inside the formation, and says the condition of the wood is what makes it interesting. Genesis describes the Ark coated in pitch, which burns easily, so the release suggests someone may have tried to set the Ark on fire long ago. Charring slows decomposition in soil, often to well under 1% a year, so “what was meant to destroy it may have actually preserved it,” the release says. The group also says the wood is not recent surface debris and was not carried in by mudflow, because it came from deep within the formation. The release allows other explanations for the charring, including lightning or volcanic activity. Founder Andrew Jones said the wood could be the charred remains of the Ark or the remains of a campfire a shepherd lit while using it for shelter centuries ago. The wood has been sent for carbon-14 dating and species identification, and the team says no firm conclusions should be drawn until the results are published. Dating would give the wood’s age and identification would show what kind of tree it came from, but neither result would by itself show that it came from a boat. Everything here comes from the group itself. The radar results are preliminary, the masking is the team’s own processing, and none of it has been through independent peer review. A 1996 study by geologist Lorence Collins and Ark hunter David Fasold concluded that Durupınar is a natural rock formation. Noah’s Ark Scans also sells guided tours and merchandise, is running a GiveSendGo fundraiser for more core drilling, and its release asks for donations and points readers to a gold dealer and a preparedness retailer. More radar processing and reporting is expected in the coming months, and Jones has said initial lab results are expected over the winter. Atila has said photos of the wood will be released in the near future.

articles.content: A 25-year-old in 2026 is starting adult life in worse shape than a 25-year-old in 2010, at least by their own account. Gallup’s newest wellbeing report finds that 44% of U.S. adults ages 18 to 29 are “thriving” so far this year, down from a high of 64% in 2010. Gallup counts someone as thriving if they rate their current life a 7 or higher on a zero-to-10 ladder and expect to rate their life an 8 or higher five years from now. Most of the drop came recently. About two-thirds of the total decline has happened since 2019. Gallup is careful about causes, saying a set of factors “may explain” the decline among young adults. It points to a rise in depression, weaker close relationships, less daily enjoyment and less feeling active and productive each day. It also lists lower satisfaction with living standards, with leaders who create enthusiasm about the future and with progress toward personal goals. Among adults 30 to 44, it says the share currently having or being treated for depression is up 15 points since 2019, to 37%. Beyond those measures, Gallup names loneliness, which it says has been particularly acute among younger men, along with housing affordability and fear of losing jobs to AI. About half of adults 18 to 49 doubt Medicare and Social Security will be available in 10 years, far more than other age groups. Just 14% of adults 18 to 34 say they are “extremely proud” to be American, down 10 points since 2025. The numbers follow people as they age. Adults now 34 to 46 are at 46%, compared with 64% when they were the 18-to-29 group in 2010, so their ratings fell as they got older while the young adults behind them are starting from a lower place. Adults 30 to 44 are at 45%, down from a high of 62% in 2016 and 2017. Adults 45 to 64 are at 46%, which matches their low from 2008. The estimates come from three Gallup Panel surveys in February, May and August 2026 with 15,156 U.S. adults in total.

articles.content: Franni Cash was about 13 when she says the community her family belonged to officially became a cult. She was 17 when her family left it. She told RELEVANT that her parents joined after their marriage hit a rough patch and a friend suggested counseling. The therapist they saw, she said, was “dangerously smart” and used people’s vulnerabilities “to kind of tether loyalty to himself.” Counseling sessions became Bible studies with other families, and then she says they were told they no longer needed church. Eventually the leader declared himself their spiritual father and warned that anyone who broke covenant with him would be cut off, and women who disagreed with their husbands were said to have “the Jezebel spirit.” “It just became so far away from the truth,” Cash said. She kept a diary about how strange it all felt. The leader found it and burned it. She was 14. “From that place I pushed it down,” she said. “I can’t question it and can’t voice this anymore.” Her family left in the middle of her senior year of high school, after an article exposed years of alleged fraud and sexual allegations tied to the leader. She remembers her parents telling the kids in their bedroom. “It was like this weight flew off my shoulders,” she said. Then came a harder year, when she feared the curses and watched her brothers struggle. “I didn’t know if I was gonna make it. I really mean that.” Her parents put the family in therapy immediately. Talk therapy alone didn’t work for her, because she was still so brainwashed she didn’t know what she could say. EMDR and brainspotting did. She has been in consistent therapy for ten years now and says talking about the cult no longer stings. “I’ve had to grieve them being susceptible to something so harmful,” she said of her parents. “But right off the bat, they got themselves in therapy.” She describes her healing journey as medicine and scripture working together. “You can’t just slap a Bible verse on it,” she said. “Scripture is so powerful, but sometimes you don’t know how to absorb it until you can do some surgery.” The family’s first song came a year and a half after they left, and it became We the Kingdom. Cash said the band was a place where she felt understood, because her family were the only people who could laugh at the jokes instead of being horrified. She also says they were trauma bonded, and that she needed to learn who she was on her own. She left the band, and says she and her family are now the closest they’ve ever been, “from a health and respect” place that “doesn’t feel enmeshed.” Her solo debut, Here I Am , takes its title from a lyric she and her father, producer and songwriter Ed Cash, wrote together for the song “The Real Thing”: Here I am, I made it through. The page is burned, but this story is not over. Here I Am was also going to be the title of an album she planned at 16, in the middle of everything. “Now here I am, kind of on the other side of healing,” she said. Getting there meant relearning music. A friend, the writer Paul Duncan, told her she needed to “date music like you would your spouse,” meaning listen to records she loved as a kid with no goal. She was driving on the Pacific Coast Highway when U2’s “Where the Streets Have No Name” came on. “It was like I heard music for the first time,” she said. She has since been listening to Marvin Gaye’s What’s Going On , Al Green, Elton John, Casey Musgraves, John Mayer and Linkin Park’s Hybrid Theory . Her view of God changed too. “I just really thought that God was this angry man upstairs,” she said. She remembers being told to get off the worship stool because she wasn’t “anointed enough.” Then she met what she calls the real Jesus. “He was so loving. And gracious with me,” she said. “It changed everything.” When we asked what she’d say to someone inside a controlling church, her answer was short. “Leave. You’re free to. articles.content: The search bar in a Bible app works like any other, which means it shows what people are worried about before they’ve said it out loud to anyone. YouVersion says “Psalm 91” was the single most-searched term in the app this year. In its newest release , the company also says “anxiety,” “hope” and “healing” were among the year’s most searched terms. YouVersion describes Psalm 91 as a psalm that encourages readers to turn to God for refuge and comfort in difficult times. The psalm runs 16 verses. Together, YouVersion says, the searches offer a glimpse into the personal questions and hopes people are bringing to Scripture. Daily use of the Bible App grew by more than 13% compared with 2025, reaching 18.5 million people a day. It also says it added more than 160 million new installs across its family of apps in 2026, after celebrating one billion installs last November. Daily engagement grew faster than installs, which the company reads as a sign that people are returning to the app and not only downloading it. Some of the highest engagement is outside the U.S. YouVersion says it sees some of the highest levels of Bible App engagement in Sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and Southeast Asia, and it is building regional hubs in places including the United Kingdom, Brazil, Kenya and Mexico. Its apps offer 3,800 versions of the Bible in 2,400 languages, and it works with a network of more than 45,000 churches and partners. Bobby Gruenewald, YouVersion’s founder and CEO, said in the release that the company has been encouraged by “how many people are turning to Scripture for answers to their questions.”

articles.title: Fear Itself
articles.summary: Widow's Bay  and the Trolley Problem of Life   The post  Fear Itself  appeared first on  Mockingbird .
articles.title_zh: 恐惧自身
articles.content: W hat is your biggest fear? Spiders? That’s a classic. Deranged clowns? Sure! Maybe you prefer the more existential variety? How about never fully realizing your potential or dying alone? All of the above? Similar to the What superpower would you choose? question, it is hard for me to select only one. I am a fearful person. I have a way of collecting fears as I go about my life. Alpha-gal, something I did not know existed until two days ago, is the flavor of the week. But my fear of dying alone is more like a longtime, trusted companion. The world is a scary place. At any moment, our identities could be hacked. Our phones could ring with dreadful news. Our brains could suffer an aneurysm. Swimming in a bottomless sea of insecurity, we are meagerly equipped with our basic survival instincts: fight, flight, freeze, and appease. These impulses may help keep us safe from spiders and clowns (answer for both: flight!), but what do we make of the dangers that are harder to pin down? What if the dangers are not only without but within? Leave it to this year’s hit TV series to explore these questions. If you’re looking for a spooky show to get into this weekend, it’s Widow’s Bay. The Emmy-sweeping, genre-bending, horror-comedic series is a triumph for a number of reasons. For starters, it muddles the black-and-white worlds Hollywood has created (e.g., horror movies without humor, comedies without any depth), reminding us that life can be both scary and funny. The show has all the irresistible horror tropes (the harbinger who warns everyone of impending doom, the suspenseful music, the jump scares) but, along with its crowd-pleasing antics, it dives deeper than surface-level fears. Its anthropology is refreshingly low. This is not a match between good people and evil monsters. Yes, sometimes the enemy is a chainsaw-wielding fiend. Much scarier, however, is when the enemy is yourself. Take Tom Loftis, for instance, the ambitious new mayor who wants to transform the cursed island town of Widow’s Bay into the next Martha’s Vineyard. He is, from every angle, a secular man. For Tom, God is no more real than ghosts. The only higher power that exists is the one you achieve by climbing the ladder. He resents how the locals tolerate the town’s haunted reputation. For too long, people have been resigned to the rumors that the hotel is haunted, the church is cursed, and the bay isn’t safe for a swim. For Tom, the only thing to fear is fear itself. Like any mayor with a messiah complex, he sets out to do something about it. As Loftis sees things, the real problem with the place is not that it is demonically possessed. The real problem is bad branding . In his eyes, Widow’s Bay is simply misunderstood. When visiting Widow’s Bay to write a piece for the New York Times travel section, a reporter asks Loftis about a framed article in the historical society titled “Cannibalism in God’s House.” Loftis tries to water it down. “These stories get so exaggerated over time,” he says. “Was there a deadly storm in 1786? Yes. Did a group of people get trapped inside a church? Apparently so. Did they immediately turn to cannibalism? No, that took four days !” See? That’s not so bad, right? Loftis’ PR campaign is like slapping new siding on a haunted mansion. He is convinced that the plight of Widow’s Bay can be solved by installing a proper cappuccino machine in the local coffee shop. Cappuccino machines are great at making a proper latte but pretty useless when up against the occult. Before long, Loftis’ denial of the curse over the island town is just as dangerous as the curse itself. The first step to keeping the forces at bay is to admit they exist. There is a scene in which Loftis speaks to another character about the Trolley Problem, an ethical thought experiment in which there is a runaway trolley barreling down the tracks toward a crowd of people. articles.title: A Crazy Train Crying in the Wilderness
articles.summary: Ozzy Osbourne's Plea to Be Heard   The post  A Crazy Train Crying in the Wilderness  appeared first on  Mockingbird .
articles.title_zh: 疯狂的火车在荒野中哭泣
articles.content: No matter who won or lost the last big game you attended, chances are, Ozzy Osbourne was there in electronic chains, locked inside a brain-rattling sound system, unnoticed, unnamed, misunderstood, a voice crying in the wilderness of crowded rows of fans desperate for a win, cheering for their heroes while jeering at their opponents, paying too much for unnecessary carbs and calories, possibly on the sabbath day. When Ozzy cried, “All aboard!” you stood with hundreds or thousands of tangential warriors singing along with the fatalistic chorus, air guitaring with the riffs, nodding with the rhythm, but you weren’t there for music. You were there to shout, thump your chest, flex, thrust hands with fingers contorted into symbols of specific allegiance, or claim you’re #1, convinced that the song, the battle cry, and the power behind it all were on your side. The words didn’t matter. Your heroes were fighting for you, to give you hope. You’d fight for them if you could, if you had to, against whoever stands in your way, to win at all costs. But what if that’s not what Ozzy wanted? How do we know what he wanted? He screams, “You’ve got to listen to my words!” Below is a paraphrase of the “Crazy Train” lyrics: “It’s crazy, but it’s always been like this — we’re all living as enemies. But maybe it’s not too late to learn how to love and forget how to hate. We’ve all got mental wounds that aren’t healing. I’m losing it. I’ve listened to everyone — fools, preachers, anarchists. Nothing helps. There’s always a system run by someone who’s a product of the system and has been conditioned to run the system, which is sold to us by rich people who get richer by keeping the system alive. And we buy it, screaming in pain from our open mental wounds. It’s messed up. I’m messed up. We’re all messed up. We inherit each other’s trouble. We’re heirs of unresolved conflict. I keep saying it, but no one listens. You’ve got to listen to my words. I can’t figure out how to feel. The mental wounds don’t heal. I don’t know who to blame, but I know it’s not fair.” I wrote the above paraphrase to read to my senior literature class last Monday morning. Nearly half of the students in the class are varsity football starters chasing championships and full-rides. I prefaced the reading with a white lie, “I got this message from someone you all know over the weekend. I won’t tell you who it is, but I want you to help me think through how to respond.” The starting quarterback, worried, tried to interrupt me. I didn’t look up, held my hand out to pause questions, and continued reading. When I finished, there was a chorus of concern from several voices: That’s a cry for help! Is it from a boy or a girl? You said we know them? Who is it? Did they email you? What did you say? They need help. Who are you going to talk to? Still in character, I said, “I can’t tell you a name, but I’ll play this song.” A few seconds into “Crazy Train,” the students realized what was going on, looked relieved, but then became uncomfortable when I turned down the volume and read out the actual lyrics. In confused silence, their faces said, We weren’t listening . I felt bad. I smiled and apologized for manipulating their emotions, and the air lightened. Someone started singing the chorus, and we moved on. But I’m not sure we should have. “Crazy Train” is the most popular song from the most recognizable sex, drugs, and rock-n-roll villain to ever bite the head off a bat, but it’s also a cry for help from a struggling human admitting personal weakness and claiming no superiority. While suggesting that love is better than hate, he’s doing more than just asking us to love. He’s asking us to LEARN HOW TO. articles.title: East Coker and the Cure for Human Inability
articles.summary: "... to be restored, our sickness must grow worse."   The post  East Coker and the Cure for Human Inability  appeared first on  Mockingbird .

articles.content: H ow strange that one can read the same poems countless times and discover new things with each visit, like a traveler coming home for Christmas only to find it slightly altered! It is the same for me revisiting T. S. Eliot’s Four Quartets : the end is different than I imagined in the beginning when I first read these words, imagined these places, and attempted to grasp the author’s meaning. Eliot had the same experience. The meaning of the Four Quartets was one thing when he originally envisioned them, another when he wrote them, and still another when the public began analyzing them. He never believed they would be forever linked with the world’s most destructive war. He had not even known there would be four. In the beginning, there was only “Burnt Norton,” written in 1936 and intended to be a one-off. It was generally well received by critics, and the whole business could have been over then. But three years passed, and Eliot found himself with that most common of authorly ailments: not knowing what to write or fearing that he no longer knew how to write properly. Specifically, he had gone for some time without constructing new poems. The world had changed since “Burnt Norton” was published. A growing menace once possible to ignore had exploded into a firestorm of destructive force sweeping through the nations of Europe, consuming all in its path. The bonds that had knit together what remained of Western Christian civilization were snapping with wild abandon, supplanted by ideologies of extermination. Faced with such a crisis, Eliot searched for the one fixed point amid the whirling chaos. He settled on the village of East Coker in Somerset, England. His ancestor Andrew Eliot had left there in 1669, abandoning the historic family home and immigrating to New England. Nearly three centuries later, Thomas Stearns Eliot had become the first member of the family to move back to the motherland, and the family connection held spiritual significance for him. In 1937, he visited St. Michael and All Angels’ Church in East Coker, where his ashes would one day be placed. I know something of Eliot’s experience. I too am the descendant of Englishmen and women whose bones lie buried in every corner of that land, some in tombs I have visited. I too was the first person in my family to return and live in England, if only for a year. It did feel in a sense like returning to my beginning, which is probably why I connect so strongly with the Four Quartets . The secret Eliot discovered at East Coker is one that has transformed my own life as well: we do not possess the power to redeem ourselves or the world and are utterly dependent on the gift of grace. Of all the Four Quartets , this is the most law and gospel poem. The Four Quartets are commonly associated with the four traditional elements of the physical world: air, earth, water, and fire. But as I have noted, Eliot did not begin with a grand plan, so the elemental symbolism becomes stronger in the later poems. Yes, we see the movement of air in “Burnt Norton” disturbing a bowl of rose leaves and carrying the laughter of children, but you would not conclude “This is an air poem” unless you had the other three Quartets to guide you. Likewise, the earth theme is not obvious after the first section of “East Coker,” but once we get to “The Dry Salvages,” we will be drowned in water imagery, and “Little Gidding” will pelt us with fire from beginning to end. Thus, Eliot begins “East Coker” rooted in the earth, in time and place and home. But immediately, the earth is overturned by the machinations of human societies succeeding and supplanting one another, building up to heaven and returning to dust. In my beginning is my end. In succession Houses rise and fall, crumble, are extended, Are removed, destroyed, restored, or in their place Is an open field, or a factory, or a by-pass. articles.content: Listeners will have a better idea of why The Mockingcast works (or doesn’t) and why they keep tuning in, 11 years later. We included a few such stories at the beginning of the 300 th episode , and the tears I shed were real. But I thought take the opportunity to offer a few observations from behind the curtain about what I personally appreciate about our podcast, what I’m most proud of, and what’s been challenging. No doubt my co-hosts would have other aspects they’d highlight. First, the longevity. It’s worth celebrating, even if it’s both a blessing and a curse. The time has allowed us to develop some pretty priceless chemistry. When I’m picking articles for us to talk about, I know that even if the material falls flat, I can rely on our dynamic to take up the slack. I trust my co-hosts, and it’s been very gratifying to watch us gel in a non-contrived way over the years. We’ve been through a lot together, and it shows, I think. Being around so long (in internet years) means we’ve had the benefit of watching things come and go. Sarah mentioned this recently in relation to the moralization of food in our society. It was super acute about eight years ago, then it retreated a bit with the body-positivity moment, now it’s back again under the guise of #maxxing. But that’s just one example. I could mention radical atheism, or gospel-centered this and that, or mindfulness. We’ve seen cultural fixations take hold and then recede, specific anxieties bubble up and dissipate. The longer view allows for a measure of perspective that I believe lends the show added depth. Longevity can also be a curse. The ebb and flow can foster a degree of detachment that masquerades as superiority. For example, it’s hard to take the latest rebranding of medieval monasticism (or justification by works) seriously when you’ve seen it happen four times under four different (best-selling) names already. Discipline becomes application becomes virtue becomes formation and so on. It’s a challenge to keep listening and paying attention, but a challenge that I’m proud of us for at least trying to live up to. Because beneath every one of the trends we’ve observed are real people with real hopes and dreams and disappointments. The second longevity-related challenge is the same one that afflicts anyone in a public role, especially those in ministry or thought life. It’s the danger of impersonating yourself. Whenever I detect in my voice any sense of “the grace guy needs to say a grace thing now” — it makes my skin crawl. Autopilot is the enemy, along with its cousin repetition. I remember a trusted listener once warning me that we were becoming a podcast about social media. Another said we were talking too much about parenting. These grooves are understandable, but to keep things fresh, especially over the long haul, you have to always be finding fresh vistas, not just in the culture but in yourself. It’s not easy. This leads me to the next observation: over ten years, it’s become notably more difficult to find suitable material for The Mockingcast . One of the things that I hold sacred about our show is its role as a refuge from culture wars. I want listeners to be confident that when they press play, we’re not going to trigger them about the same headlines that trigger them the rest of the day. We haven’t done this perfectly, I realize, but it remains a guiding principle. When the occasional how-dare-you emails come in, folks are usually surprised to hear that they come just as frequently from both sides of the aisle. If they didn’t, I’d try to course correct. Finding stuff that threads the needle of interesting and substantial but not pre-narrativized has gotten more challenging over our tenure. It’s like the ledge we walk has gotten narrower. Not nonexistent, mind you, just narrower. I’m so proud we’ve reached this milestone without, at least in my view, falling into an ideological ditch or becoming (too) predictable. articles.content: “You only work on Sundays, anyway.” One of the go-to jokes of a group of guys I hang out with. I laugh because, well, I just like to please people. But every time the boys say it, I think to myself, “If you only knew what being a pastor feels like sometimes.” An impromptu funeral at the clinic for veterinarians whose colleague committed suicide, scrolling to find an angry email about last week’s sermon or the changing of the carpet color in the narthex, begging financial generosity from people who pay your salary, lunch with a lonely man going through a brutal divorce, restocking the youth fridge with 7,000 Cheerwines, hearing that they’re gossiping about you again, failing yet again to prepare a sermon that marries TikTok and TED Talk, off to the shelter to serve dinner, did I even eat lunch? Did I mention that this was last Tuesday? Ministry is often pure gift. The highs are as high as they get. Pastors bear witness to the most intimate, most raw, most human, most beautiful and terrifying moments of people’s lives. We play at the level of the soul. We get paid to read and write and pray. We have a front-row seat to miracles: the bound freed, the sinner forgiven, the debts paid, the dead resurrected. It’s not lost on me that having a job rife with meaning is a privilege and honor. This is what God has chosen to make of my life, and I am truly grateful. And yet, there’s no way to get away from the fact that ministry is a burden too. Its shape is a cross. Its form is death and resurrection. People bring all their junk to church — and they should. Sunday mornings are not an assembly of the righteous, they are a sanctuary for sinners — hypocrites anonymous, I like to call it. One of the chief problems that has arisen in my ministry is that I find it so hard to be ministered to. Ministers minister, preachers preach, consolers console, but if you’re not careful, a pastor will find herself without a pastor, a preacher will find himself without a preacher. Everyone needs both. Not long ago I burnt out. Years after, I realize the burnout was not the product of overwork. The fire in my soul was extinguished because for years I had offered relief to others without finding ways to receive it myself. What becomes of a healer who forsakes his own wounds? Pay attention when your soul stops singing. And I did. I prayed for God to bring relief, somehow, someway. And then, to quote Morgan Freeman in The Shawshank Redemption , “a beautiful little bird flew into my drab little cage.” That beautiful bird was Mockingbird Ministries. And now for six years I have done what Michael Gershon calls “staking one’s life on the rumors of grace.” As the 300th of the Mockingcast draws near, I thought it fitting to say what Mbird has been for me: My theological home: Pastors in the mainline will tell you that our denominations are fracturing. It’s tempting to give in to extremes and to weaponize politics toward ecclesial ends. This has made me feel like I don’t belong anywhere politically, theologically, or pastorally. I know many fellow pastor Mbirders agree because we’ve talked about it. Pastors in the mainline who long for a ministry rooted only in the gospel are like an island of misfit toys. Mbird has become for us a gracious home and a place to be reminded again and again of the gospel of grace. My Preacher: I listen to the Mockingcast on Monday mornings. You pastors out there know Monday’s malaise. Dizzied and frenzied from all of Sunday’s work and pressured by a million regrets about the sermon or the attendance, I find sweet relief in the words of RJ, Sarah, and Dave. “That’s right,” I think. “This is what ministry about.” God may not speak to us all through an audible voice in our heads, but God does speak through the words of a sermon. articles.content: 1. “ ‘I Shall Be Very Surprised If There Isn’t A Next Chapter’ ” is the title of the remarkable interview with English theologian Sarah Coakley that appeared on the New York Times website this past week, courtesy of Peter Wehner. We’ve been at this Another Week Ends game for a couple decades now, and I’m not sure I’ve ever seen so much theological substance published in America’s once-and-future(?) paper of record. I’ve been aware of Coakley’s work and reputation for some time but never taken the plunge, which, after reading their conversation, feels like a bit of a shame-on-me situation. One of my favorite bits comes at the very beginning, when Coakley talks about her teenage years. Apparently the confirmation classes at her little Church of England parish lacked the rigor she was hoping for. Thus, she did what all kids that age do these days: My eldest brother and I organized our own theological discussion group in that same parish. We brought a lot of our atheistical and skeptical school friends into it. And this very holy rector was very clever at this point, because he just sat watching the arguments go backward and forward, rather like the umpire at Wimbledon. He never intervened, never put us right, never told us what the right answer was. When my brother and I recently thought about who had attended those discussions, the vast majority of our friends who attended at that age, 14 to 16, subsequently became Christians. So that tells you something about opening the Pandora’s box theologically and how important it is for the clergy not to stifle that. A lovely little testament to the power of grace in practice, I’d say, and one which jibes with my own decades working with young people. Allow students to ask their questions, raise their objections and air their doubts without threat of defensiveness — let that stuff hang in the air — and the craziest things can happen, especially over the long haul. Squash their arguments with doctrine, even right doctrine, and you risk alienating them forever. Such is the emotional wallop of correction, however well intentioned. Coakley goes on to provide some rather damning commentary on the gap in theology between the academy and the pew, the professor and the layperson. One of the core hopes of her own work, she claims, is the closing of that gap chasm, to which I can only add a hearty amen. I’ve tried to do something similar in my own books, albeit on a much smaller scale. (Whether utilizing a French phrase for that project — théologie totale — screams accessibility is a separate question.) In Coakley’s view, uncoupling the study of theology from the practice of prayer is dangerous. This leads her into one of the most beautiful articulations of prayer I’ve read anywhere, let alone the New York Times : How do I pray? Well, you hand yourself over to the source of your being, and then you ask some things. But the handing over is primary, and learning how to do that. It changes your perspective on God — because when you practice this, even for a very short time each day, simple opening up space in which God is God. You don’t control it. That’s what’s so frightening. This is not a new skill, like learning how to make a very good omelet or to ride a bicycle. This is a nonskill. It’s an unskilling, an unmastery. It completely changes your view of God, because up to that point you’ve probably subliminally been thinking about God as a very large entity, the largest and the best in a universe of entities whom somehow you’ve got to get on your side or cajole or get to answer your request. I know that’s a very naïve sounding description, but as a priest I can tell you that’s the God I hear about all the time. All the great theologians of the tradition have slain that God, and they’ve had to slay that God — think of Luther — with great terror. It’s really just opening up to the possibility of grace. articles.content: Welcome back, fiends! Blaine Grimes, Blake Collier, Caleb Stallings, and I are back with the Spooky Season film roundtable, and this week we are watching John Carpenter’s In the Mouth of Madness , the third of his “Apocalypse” films. So file in to Row D, your seat’s a few down from ours and right next to Sam Neill, who’s gulping down popcorn and drawing more crosses on his face. Let’s go a little crazy! Ian : Caleb, what led you to pick In the Mouth of Madness ? Caleb : I actually watched it earlier this year on my quest to see every John Carpenter film. This was the final movie of his I hadn’t seen. And it was the perfect one to end on. An autumnal, meta movie about authorship and terror. Just right up my alley. And what better way to go insane than in an impossibly dark cathedral in an autumnal New England town? Who wouldn’t want to watch a movie about that? And who wouldn’t want it to happen to them too? Ian : Well, when you put it that way … Blake : I was really struck this time by Trent and Cane’s dialogue when Cane states, “I am God now …” and Trent responds something to the effect of “I didn’t know God was a hack horror writer.” It’s a great comeback but also chilling in that humans, no matter their brilliance and no matter how well-adjusted they present as being, are hacks when it comes to authoring their own stories, let alone the stories of others. Only God can weave the narrative in such a way that the goodness, justice, and mercy of the ending is earned. Caleb : And that sanity is maintained! Blake : Exactly! Caleb : If fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, then trying to usurp him is entering the Mouth of Madness. Ian : It is, but it’s a sanity that might look insane to the surrounding world. And that’s the question with Trent, isn’t it? He sounds insane, but he sees through the bogus story Cane is weaving. Blake : In this way, I think the film makes for a thrilling blueprint of the failures of humans trying to weave together the grand narrative of existence, and how fiction can portray our own failures to usurp God’s position and role. Caleb : This reminded me of Tim Keller recounting how Dorothy Sayers wrote herself into her own detective novels to be a help and savior of a sort to her own protagonist, Peter Wimsey. In the Mouth of Madness tells the opposite story: Sutter Cane writes himself into his stories to destroy his characters. Blake : So in this way, Cane is a type of Satan … which means Dante’s footprint is all over this film as well. Blaine : *In Gordon Ramsey voice* Bloody hell. Here we go again … Ian : You know, I’m something of a Dante adaptation myself! We are all creatures spoken into existence, in a story in which, like Sayers, the Teller, the Creator, becomes a character. And there are so many stories vying for authoritative interpretation of the world and of what we are. Caleb : There’s something interesting too in how many times it’s mentioned that the film rights to Cane’s book have been optioned. I think Carpenter was playing with how many people are only familiar with these stories via the film medium, which I imagine is even more true now, 30 years later. And the movie ends, not with Trent rereading Cane’s book to find out how it all ends but rather alone in a theater, eating popcorn and laughing hysterically (almost weeping) as he watches his own life play out, rather absurdly, on the silver screen. Blake : In some ways it is the mixed moral affection of giving oneself over to something that isn’t a wholly moral good. articles.title: What Is Rest For?
articles.summary: Reflections on a Sabbatical   The post  What Is Rest For?  appeared first on  Mockingbird .
articles.title_zh: 休息的目的是什么？
articles.content: This past summer marked my eighteenth year in full-time pastoral ministry work. I have served churches in Sacramento, Hawaii, and now Minnesota (makes perfect sense). My congregation here in Bloomington (we just hosted the fall Mbird conference!) decided several years ago to establish a sabbatical policy for our pastors. A sabbatical is extended paid time off, anywhere from a month to a year, for the individual to rest and/or research. The modern versions of this started at Harvard in the late 1800s as a way for professors to have a break from the grind of classrooms to dive deeper into some form of research. In recent years, this concept has expanded to many professions, and particularly into ministry. The sabbatical I received this past summer was three months and carried no requirement for continuing ed or book writing. The goals were to unplug, rest, and spend time with family. They also wanted me to provide some reflections on the experience. Not wanting this to be a summer vacation report on steroids, I thought I would provide a general view to the experience, with some deeper reflection on the nature and purpose of rest. My hope is that you will be able to recognize God’s gifts of rest in your own life. Though I gave you the quick definition of a sabbatical, the concept is rooted in God’s Word, so I turned there first to try and make sense of the strangeness I just experienced. Leviticus isn’t the first place I think of in terms of grace and rest, and yet in chapter 25 the Lord instructs the following: “For six years sow your fields, and for six years prune your vineyards and gather their crops. But in the seventh year the land is to have a year of sabbath rest” (Lev 25:3–4). He goes on to describe how the land going a bit wild will still provide food to eat but shouldn’t be in any sense “worked on.” It sounds strange to my ears to hear that the land itself needs a break. Does it manage a life/work balance? Is there a time when it stops doing what it’s doing? Jesus doesn’t add much clarity for me on this. In one instance he tells us that the flowers don’t “labor or spin” (Matt 6). In another the plants are described as growing unceasingly: “Night and day, whether he sleeps or gets up, the seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how” (Mk 4). It’s helpful to not have clear pragmatism about the command to give land rest. We can, of course, point to studies about fallow fields. We can see that the lack of harvesting is about rest for the people. But the truth remains that God commands rest and doesn’t give us all the reasons why. The idea of sabbath is built into God’s created order. In other words, our discomfort with rest is strange, not the rest itself. Beyond Deserving But did I deserve a sabbatical? The very first Mockingbird conference I attended was in 2019 and titled: “Beyond Deserving: Hope in a World of Performance.” To say that I was at a point of burnout would be an understatement, and that conference and phrase are forever embedded in my heart. Grace is all about being beyond the question of what is deserved, and a true sabbatical is rooted in this. In the lead-up to my planned break, I tended to receive two kinds of responses from people concerning the idea. The first kind was more common and positive. Many people told me I deserved it and that pastors work hard and that I’ve earned it. These are kind words from kind people and rooted in love, and I accept them as such. But as I think about my life, I can’t say that I deserve three months of paid vacation to do what I want. Every time someone has asked about this, I feel a little uneasy and am certain there are way more deserving people who aren’t receiving such a gift. And some people told me as much! The second kind of response I received was along the lines of “Well, I pastored for 40 years and never had a break.” In other words, you young’uns are soft and you don’t deserve this sabbatical, so you shouldn’t have gotten one. articles.title_zh: 我想要相信
articles.content: The Battle of Kadesh in the thirteenth century BC, between Egypt and the Hittite Empire, was one of the great battles of the ancient world, notable for both sides making heavy use of chariots. Archaeological and textual sources indicate that Kadesh was a bloody, chaotic stalemate that nearly ended in disaster for Pharoah Ramesses II and the Egyptian army. But Ramesses knew as well as any contemporary influencer that, sometimes, you have to dress things up a bit for your followers. Accordingly, he commissioned a set of temple reliefs at various sites in Egypt and Nubia depicting himself as a gargantuan, godlike being smiting the helpless Hittite warriors in a glorious victory for Egypt. The phenomenon of false or misleading images, it turns out, long predates large language models, Photoshop, or even the camera. On the other hand, the growing ubiquity of AI-produced content has certainly exacerbated the problem. In a recent article , Tyler Austin Harper — staff writer for the Atlantic and probably my favorite lefty writer — describes his love of “wetsuiting,” that is, wading out at night to remote sandbars or rocks to fish for striped bass. Some in this niche community post pictures of their catches on Instagram. “People who fish are habitual liars,” as Harper notes, fondly, but the increasing prevalence and sophistication of AI platforms now leaves Harper and his friends questioning not only the purported size of the pictured bass but whether it even exists at all. While photoshopping otherwise genuine images has long been an issue in the angling world, Harper complains that AI’s capability to create images from scratch “automates away the need not only to photograph a fish, but to even catch one in the first place.” Combined with the “documentary impulse” to gain notoriety online for one’s (ostensible) skills, AI tools provide an avenue to impressing others without the hassle of building those skills in the first place. For Harper, the worst part of it is the reflexive skepticism engendered by the pervasiveness of AI-produced slop. It’s a very human thing to be amazed by displays of skill — but now, if “AI makes it impossible to trust what we see … [then we] have lost the ability to believe in the accomplishments of others.” To be fair, there is such a thing as “healthy” skepticism. Even without AI, there’s no end to noise, rumor, speculation passed off as fact, and half-truths percolating about the internet and airwaves. Sometimes the effects are harmless enough. During Russia’s first invasion of Ukraine (c. 2014), I came across an article that Netflix had responded by suspending Vladimir Putin’s personal account. I shared the article completely in earnest, partly because I thought it was funny, partly as an indictment of the West’s weak response to Russian aggression. I had, in fact, fallen victim to “satire,” which was embarrassing enough, but hardly damaging to myself or anyone else. Other examples are less benign, like my online ranting against Elon Musk’s perceived Nazi salute — when, as it happened, even the ADL was urging the public to give Musk the benefit of the doubt. It’s probably unlikely, but certainly not impossible, that I tipped somebody somewhere a bit more in the direction of fear and resentment, in service of venting my feelings about my own hasty interpretation of a picture. *** Again, none of this is new. The world has always contained its share of charlatans, fraudsters, and demagogues making use of fact-free propaganda. Jesus himself encourages suspicion in some situations: Then if anyone says to you, ‘Look! Here is the Messiah!’ or ‘There he is!’ — do not believe it. For false messiahs and false prophets will appear and produce great signs and wonders, to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. (Mt 24:23–24) The problem is when skepticism becomes a baseline disposition or attitude. The Kick streamer, who has 1.9 million followers on Instagram, reposted the clip in his newest post with a caption that reads: “This is from about 6 months ago. articles.title_zh: 乔纳森·艾萨克是NBA最直言不讳的基督徒之一。他最近更安静了，这是有目的的。
articles.content:
Near the end of his interview on the new RELEVANT Podcast,
Jonathan Isaac
was asked for the sound bite: one way the Lord’s been encouraging him lately, the kind of clip that does numbers on Instagram, a professional athlete saying something encouraging about faith.
Isaac laughed. “I wish it was that simple, right?”
A few years ago it might have been. Isaac, who’s starting his 10th season with the Orlando Magic, spent a stretch of his career as one of the league’s most visibly Christian players, with invitations to talk about faith on stages and broadcasts. Lately, he’s been quieter. He says that’s on purpose.
“I definitely felt the pressure of feeling like I had to speak out or say something, or kind of just wear my Christianity on my sleeve in a way that was going to make everybody else feel good,” he told RELEVANT. “And that really is tough. It’s a tough thing to deal with, even when you’re struggling in the background with faith or with your own struggles, while still having to present a certain way to other people.”
Eventually, Isaac decided to pull back.
“I’ve definitely taken a step back from being as vocal,” he said. “I don’t speak as much. I don’t do as much as I’ve done in the past, just from a standpoint of wanting to focus on myself and my relationship with Christ and growing in that way, rather than being what everybody else needs you to be.”
The pedestal problem
Isaac came to faith the way a lot of people do — church as a kid, songs and youth group and none of it his own — and then lost it to basketball, which he called “my god” from middle school through the draft. What changed him was getting everything the NBA had to offer and finding he “still felt as unfulfilled as I felt chasing the thing.” Faith became the identity that wasn’t a stat line.
As Isaac’s faith became more public, the invitations followed.
“We see somebody that agrees with us on something and they’re in some type of status,” he said, “and we want to have them out to all the speaking engagements and get them on all the podcasts and everything.”
Isaac doesn’t frame that attention as malicious. “It’s just a nature of the beast kind of thing,” he said. But it put public expectations around a faith he was still working out while, in his words, “fighting for faith, staying faithful, losing faith, all those different things.”
The way he puts it now is that following Jesus is hard enough without an audience.
“Just Christianity as a whole — it’s hard enough in today’s age to be faithful, to seek and search after God and to cultivate that relationship. It’s hard enough to do that, period,” he said. “Then to do it with eyes on you, and pressure, and people coming around for the wrong reasons, and having difficulty trusting it. It’s a lot.”
What he’d tell the next guy
The last few seasons have produced a steady stream of athletes going more public with their faith — public baptisms, online Bible studies, postgame interviews that open with Jesus. Asked whether Christian athletes talk to each other about the pressure that comes next, Isaac didn’t pretend they do.
“Man, I wish we did more than what it is,” Isaac said.
For Isaac, the important question is who is close enough to tell the truth when the platform gets bigger.
“It really is about the people that are around you, and having people that you really, really trust — especially when it comes to your leaders in a church setting,” he said. “Just having somebody where it’s not just you having this platform and navigating it by yourself. Because then, in my opinion, it’s easier to fall for that pressure of feeling like you need to present a certain way.”
When Isaac tore his ACL in 2020 and his Nike shoe deal ran out, his pastor at the time told him he should make his own shoe. So he surrounded himself with people he trusted in the industry and launched
UNITUS.
The company he founded around a basketball shoe with a Bible verse on it is now three years old, is about to cross 50,000 pairs sold and is now led by

articles.title_zh: ChatGPT每周收到超过7000万个宗教问题
articles.content:
Turns out plenty of people are asking ChatGPT to explain the hard parts of the Bible. OpenAI says it gets more than 70 million religion-related requests every week, according to
an analysis it published
Oct. 8.
About 22 million of them are about studying religious texts. Another 16 million are about practices, holidays and observance, and 16 million more are about beliefs, meaning and spiritual guidance. The analysis covers September 2025 through September 2026.
Islam accounted for roughly 45% of the requests and Christianity for 34%, with Hinduism at 4%, Judaism at 2% and Buddhism at 1%. Christianity questions spike around Easter. Islam questions spike around Ramadan and Eid al-Adha.
Among the Christianity-related messages, nearly half are about Bible passages and another 13% are about worship, sermons or church practices. OpenAI says people ask ChatGPT to explain difficult passages and find commentaries from within their tradition. The average request sounds a lot more like small group than a debate about whether God exists.
Barna has found that practicing Christians already use AI at work and at home more than most Americans, and nearly half say they’d trust it with their spiritual growth. They use it more than their pastors do, too, and only about 12% of pastors feel ready to guide them on it.
OpenAI is careful to say AI “is not — and should not become — an arbiter of religious truth.” Sam Altman, for his part, has said
he’s “very uncomfortable” with people treating AI like a religion
.
Whether any of those conversations send someone back to an actual Bible, or an actual church, is something the report doesn’t say.

articles.title_zh: 彼得·蒂尔（ Peter Thiel ）花了三年时间讲解敌基督。这是他在说什么。
articles.content:
Peter Thiel co-founded PayPal and Palantir. He is a tech investor, not a pastor or a theologian, but for the last three years he’s been giving invitation-only lectures about the Antichrist.
The audio first surfaced a year ago, when
The Washington Post
and
The Guardian
reported on recordings of the series in October 2025.
The Verge
has now published an analysis written by David Gibson, a Catholic scholar and journalist who directs the
Center on Religion and Culture at Fordham University
.
The talks started in San Francisco in 2025, and in March Thiel took a
four-part series to Rome
.
His argument hangs on 1 Thessalonians 5:3, where Paul warns about people proclaiming “peace and safety.” Thiel reads that as the Antichrist’s slogan. In his version, the people pushing safety, from AI regulation to effective altruism, are a restraining force that paves the way for the Antichrist. In the first lecture he worries Cold War II could end in an unjust peace, a peace at any price.
Then come the names. Thiel says a friend urged him to tell the room Bill Gates is the Antichrist. He calls Gates a “Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde-type” who would give his soul for a Nobel Peace Prize. Greta Thunberg is “maybe sort of a type or a shadow.” Marc Andreessen is safe, because “the Antichrist is popular.” Earlier leaked snippets have him calling Pope Leo XIV Beijing’s “useful idiot” over AI regulation, and in a July essay for
First Things
,
“The Pope and the Antichrist,”
he floats that the late Pope Francis could have been the Antichrist.
Gibson, a Catholic, reads the lectures as “a fairly standard-issue American evangelical worldview,” and a fundamentalist one at that. Thiel is in no way a church leader, and he doesn’t speak for evangelicals, most of whom wouldn’t recognize their faith in a theology that names Bill Gates and AI regulation as the Antichrist’s allies. Gibson also argues Thiel misreads Pope Benedict XVI, whose writing on the apocalypse was about the future of the church, not a countdown.
Thiel once told a San Francisco audience that keeping people out of the room is good marketing. We’re all writing about it, so he may be onto something. The rest? Probably not.
